about: Sliesthorp (Hedeby, Haithabu) at the head of the Slie, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/sliesthorp.md and the spine; a draft for the user to overwrite. Woven into the region danes_norway on 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver: ties made to run both ways, people named in ties made real in their own ports or pointed at the right id, stories given beats and cards in the other ports, and the region's cards (encounters/danes_norway_793.json) named in the sites' 'do' lists.

ports.summary: In 793 Sliesthorp is a young market on a green field at the head of the Slie, where a ship from the eastern sea can sail a long day inland and lie in a sheltered inner water a short cart road from the rivers of the western sea. There is no wall, no coin, no church and no king's name on it yet: thatched houses along a brook, booths in summer, a dealer's pen, and the old earth wall of the Danes on the ridge behind. A merchant comes for amber, furs, combs, beads and people, sells wine, cloth, querns and (if he dares) Frankish blades, and pays and is paid in silver by weight.
ports.seasons: The market is full from late May to the middle of August, when ships from the Svear, the Wends and Vestfold lie in the inner water and the carts go west every day; outside those weeks half the booths are bare poles. In autumn the cart road to the Treene turns to mud and the herring come into the Slie (?); in a hard winter the head of the Slie, which is shallow and half fresh, freezes over (?), and the place lives on fish, smoke and talk until the water opens.

history.text: The Danes fell the oaks for the North Wall of their earthwork, and about now build a barrier of log caissons across the narrows of the Slie.
history.source: de.wikipedia Danewerk; de.wikipedia Schlei-Seesperrwerk (tree-ring dates 737 to 740), as in the dossier [WDW; WSP]

history.text: About this year the first houses stand south of the brook: a trading place on a green field, without a town's fittings.
history.source: de.wikipedia Haithabu; da.wikipedia Hedeby (the southern settlement, dug from 1959) [WDE; WDA]

history.text: This year Godfred, king of the Danes, came with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom to the place called Sliesthorp, on the border of his kingdom and Saxony. He promised to meet the emperor and did not.

This year Godfred destroyed the trading place on the shore which the Danes call Reric, which by its tolls brought his kingdom great profit, carried its merchants off, and came by ship to the harbour called Sliesthorp. He stayed some days and ordered the border closed with a wall, with one gate only, through which wagons and horsemen could be sent out and let in.
This year Thrasco, prince of the Obodrites, was killed at Reric by Godfred's men.
This year two hundred ships harried Frisia and took a hundred pounds of silver, and Godfred was murdered by one of his own followers. While the emperor waited on the king's threats his elephant died.

This year peace was sworn on the Eider, twelve men a side: for the Danes the king's brothers Hancwin and Angandeo, Osfrid called Turdimulo, Warstein, Suomi, Urm, Osfrid son of Heiligen, Osfrid of Sconaowe, Hebbi and Aowin.
This year an army of Saxons and Obodrites crossed the Eider for Harald, the king who had been driven out.
Gluomi is named as warden of the Northmen's border.
About this year the first coins of the North are struck here: light pennies copied from Dorestad's.
This year Harald was baptised among the Franks, and the monk Anskar went north with him.
About this year King Horik gave leave for a church at the port of Sliaswic, with a house for its priest. After that the merchants of Dorstadt and Hamburg came freely and without fear.
history.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar 24 (tr. Robinson 1921); the year is about 849 to 850 [RIM; WDE]

history.text: This year Horik was killed in a war among his own kin. Hovi, count of the port, had the church shut, saying the gods were angry; soon the young king put him out, the church was opened, and a bell was allowed, which the heathen held unlawful.
This year the kings Sigfred and Halfdan made peace with King Louis, so that merchants of either realm might cross the border and buy and sell in peace.
history.source: Annals of Fulda 873, as given at en.wikipedia Sigfred and Halfdan (the annal itself not opened) [WSH]

history.text: About this year Ohthere of Halogaland sailed from Sciringes heal to the port the English call 'at the Heaths' in five days, and Wulfstan sailed from it to Truso in seven days and nights, under sail all the way. Both told King Alfred.
history.source: Ohthere and Wulfstan in Alfred's Orosius (Hakluyt, The Discovery of Muscovy, Cassell 1893) [OHT]; texts_793.json ohthere, wulfstan

history.text: About this year a house from the Svear's land rules here: Olaf, and after him his sons Chnob and Gyrd (?). A great man is laid in a chamber under a boat south of the houses, with two companions and three horses.
history.source: Adam of Bremen at second hand and the rune stones (de.wikipedia Runensteine von Haithabu; en.wikipedia Gyrd and Gnupa); the boat chamber grave (de.wikipedia Bootkammergrab von Haithabu) [WRS; WGG; WBK] (?)

history.text: This year King Henry beat the Danes' king Chnuba, made him pay tribute and take baptism.
history.source: Widukind, as given at de.wikipedia Runensteine von Haithabu (Widukind himself not opened) [WRS]

history.text: This year a bishop, Hored, was named for Sliaswig. Whether he ever came is not known.
history.source: de.wikipedia Hored; Liste der Bischöfe von Schleswig [WHR; WBL]

history.text: In the 960s Ibrahim ibn Yaqub of Tortosa walked the town: fish the main food, a few Christians with a church, a sacrifice hung on poles at the yard gate, women free to divorce, both sexes with painted eyes, and singing like the howling of dogs.
history.source: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub (al-Tartushi) as given at en.wikipedia Hedeby; he travelled 961-962, the page says 965 [WEN; WIB]

history.text: About this year the Connection Wall joins the town's half-ring rampart (begun after 930) to the old Danes' wall.
This year the emperor Otto took the border and the wall. In 983 the Danes took them back.

About this year a king's longship is built here, some thirty-one metres long and under three metres wide. Years later she is burnt to the waterline as a fire ship in the harbour (the year is given two ways).
About this year warriors sat round the town. King Svein raised a stone for Skarthi, his retainer, 'who had fared west and now fell at Hedeby'; Thorolf raised one for his partner Erik, a steersman.
history.source: the rune stones of Haithabu (de.wikipedia Runensteine von Haithabu); the siege has no year [WRS]

history.text: About this year Harald of Norway burned the town from end to end with fire ships.
history.source: en.wikipedia Hedeby; de.wikipedia Haithabu (Harald's poet) [WEN; WDE]

history.text: This year West Slavs sacked and burned what was left, and the people moved over the Slie to Sliaswic on the north shore. The empty ring was afterwards called Oldenburg, the old fort.

eras.text: A market on a green field. A dozen long thatched houses south of the brook, booths in summer, boats drawn up or lying to stakes in the inner water. No wall, no coin, no king's man with a name: gifts are given to whoever speaks for the place, silver goes on the scales, and a stranger needs a host. Asulf's pen is the biggest roof on the strand.

Godfred's years. In 804 the Slie is full of the king's ships and the heath of his horses: fodder, ale and bread are dear. In 808 the merchants of Reric are set down on the strand with what they could carry, plots are paced out with a knotted rope, and a wall is dug and timbered across the neck with one gate and the king's man at it. Every guest owes days on the wall. In 810 the fleet goes west and the king does not grow old.

After the peace on the Eider. The Wends' plots have houses on them and children who speak Danish. Kings change and fight each other; the gate stays, and so does the toll at it. A warden keeps the border. Dirhams from the east are cut up on the scales beside Frankish pennies and arm rings.

The king's own pennies are struck here, copied from Dorestad's, letters and all, and pass by count on the strand. Horik is sole king from about 828. From 834 men in the harbour sell Dorestad cloth with the lead seal still on it, and Dorestad people, and the king says the fleets are not his. A new row of houses stands north of the brook and plank streets run down to the jetties.

A wooden church by the harbour and a priest's house. Merchants baptised at Dorstadt and Hamburg hear Mass openly; others take the sign of the cross and leave baptism for their deathbed. After Horik's death in 854 the count nails the door shut; then it opens again and a bell is allowed. Anskar comes and goes until he dies in 865.

Peace with the Saxons' king: merchants cross the border freely. The town is at its busiest, the middle settlement on the brook: comb-makers, bead-makers, a glass furnace, smiths, weavers. An Englishman and a Northman from the far north meet on the jetties and each says how many days he sailed.

Kings of a house from the Svear's land (?). Great men are buried with horses and a boat. In 934 the Saxon king beats Chnuba and takes tribute and a baptism from him. After 930 a half-ring of turf and ditch goes up round the houses, running out into the water as a row of piles.

A bishop is named for the place, at least on parchment. Harald is king and is baptised about 965. A traveller from Spain finds a great town at the far end of the world sea, eating fish and singing badly. The rampart is joined to the old wall. From 974 the emperor's men hold the border and tribute goes south.

The Danes hold their gate again. Svein and then Cnut are kings; from 991 English pennies are everywhere, and men come home from England with more than they can spend. About 1000 warriors sit round the town and stones are raised for the dead. The rampart stands as high as four men. Big ships no longer like the shallow inner water.

About 1050 Harald of Norway burns the town from end to end. People build again, smaller, inside the black ring. In 1066 the Wends come and it is finished: the last families carry their gear over the Slie to the north shore.

sites.name: The brook-mouth landing
sites.see: A still, brown inner water ringed with reeds, a brook running out over a strand of sand and mussel shell. In front, small clinker boats drawn up on rollers and bigger ships lying to stakes in the shallows; a short timber jetty where the brook has cut a channel. Behind, thatch and smoke on a green slope. Wet rope, tar, fish guts, a hammer on rivets somewhere, gulls arguing over the gutting place. In later years the jetties run sixty paces out and a row of piles closes the harbour.
sites.source: The harbour in the Noor before the brook mouth, 11 ha, later with a pile barrier and jetties up to 60 m (de.wikipedia Haithabu; da.wikipedia Hedeby). The jetty of 793 is the game's assumption (dossier 1) (?). The gift to the place's spokesman stands for a toll no source records (lore/law_tolls.md 11)

sites.name: The booths by the brook
sites.see: Two rows of booths of poles and sailcloth along the brook, the ground between them trodden to black mud and laid with split planks. On the boards: furs in bundles of forty, lumps of yellow amber, combs, glass beads on strings, whetstones, soapstone pots, a Frankish cup nobody can afford. Every seller has a folding scale and a bag of weights. Buyers nick silver with a knife before it goes in the pan. Five tongues at once, and the smell of wet fur, ale and smoke.
sites.source: Goods of Norway, Sweden, Ireland, the east Baltic and Francia; Arab silver (de.wikipedia Haithabu; en.wikipedia Hedeby). Scales, weights and the knife nick: economy/silver_coin.md and lore/law_tolls.md (finds at Birka, Hedeby, Kaupang); not opened in the dossier (?)

sites.name: The dealer's pen
sites.see: A fenced yard above the strand with a roof along one side and a water trough. People sit under the roof in rows, some in iron fetters, most only tired. A row of notched sticks hangs on a peg by the gate, one for each ship that sold here this year. On a bench outside lie the odd things that came with the lots: a sealskin, two cups, a bell without a tongue. It is quiet. The dealer's hazel switch taps his boot while he talks.
sites.source: Slaves and iron fetters at Hedeby (de.wikipedia Haithabu); Anskar bought Danish and Slav boys (Rimbert 15); Rimbert bought Christians back here about 870 (Vita Rimberti 17-18, lore/law_tolls.md) (?). The pen and its keeper are invented (spine cast.asulf)

sites.name: The ferry on the Slie
sites.see: A tarred four-oared boat at a stake on the north side of the houses, where the inner water opens into the Slie. Across the grey water, a low shore of reeds and oak wood, and smoke from farms. The ferryman sits in the stern with a small bag tied under his seat. Further out, where the Slie narrows, a dark line of logs shows at low water, and a ship is feeling for the gap in it. Curlews, the knock of oars, cold air off the water.
sites.source: The Slie, its broads and narrows (de.wikipedia Schlei); the timber sea barrier of about 737-740 off Reesholm, how ships passed it unknown (de.wikipedia Schlei-Seesperrwerk). The ferry and ferryman are the spine's (riddle_road hook); riddles_793.json r-gest-23 is given by a ferryman on the Schlei

sites.name: Gunnhild's house
sites.see: A long house of wattle and reed thatch, the door on the lee side, a fire down the middle and benches along both walls. Sea chests under the benches, a gaming board scratched on a plank, notched sticks stuck in the wall above the ale vat: one for each guest who has not paid. A back room behind a hanging. Smoke in the roof, sour mash, wet wool drying, somebody singing low in his throat and nobody asking him to stop.
sites.source: Houses of timber and wattle with reed roofs, 3.5 by 17 m to 7 by 17.5 m (de.wikipedia Haithabu). Gaming pieces at Hedeby: story/town_games_793.json (from memory there) (?). The singing: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, 960s. The house and its keeper are invented

sites.name: The slip under the alders
sites.see: A strip of shore north of the brook, black with old tar. A hull stands on blocks, half planked, her ribs not yet in: the planks are split oak, thin as a hand, and overlap like the scales of a fish. A boy heats rivets. Wood chips float along the water's edge, and a pile of oak logs lies under wet hides to keep it green. The wright walks round her with an axe and does not seem to measure anything.
sites.source: Boat-builders among the town's crafts (haithabu-danewerk.de); Hedeby 1 was built here about 985 (en.wikipedia Hedeby 1); story/ships_793.json lists sliesthorp as a building place. The slip and its wright are invented

sites.name: The pit-houses
sites.see: Small sunken huts on the north-west edge, each a roof on the ground with a doorway and a man working in the light of it. A comb-maker saws antler into plates, ankle-deep in white shavings; next door a bead-maker turns a rod of glass in a clay oven no bigger than a beehive. Amber chips, bone dust, charcoal smoke, the whine of a small saw. At one yard gate two poles stand with a ram's hide hanging between them.
sites.source: Pit-houses as workshops; over 340,000 pieces of comb-makers' waste; 7,700 beads of carnelian, crystal, amber, jet and glass; a domed oven on a burnt pit-house; a glass furnace of 850-900; goldsmiths' mercury (en.wikipedia Hedeby; de.wikipedia Haithabu; da.wikipedia Hedeby). The sacrifice poles at a yard gate are Ibrahim's, 960s, carried back to 793 (?)

sites.name: The cart road and the one gate
sites.see: A rutted road leaving the houses westward along the foot of a long grassy bank: the Danes' old wall, taller than a rider, its oak front grey with age. Ox-carts wait in a line, loaded with bales and casks for the landing on the Treene, a long day west. From 808 there is new earth and raw timber on the bank, and a single gate wide enough for one wagon, with the king's man beside it and a tally stick in his hand. Dust, dung, axle grease, an ox lowing.
sites.source: The Main Wall, North Wall and East Wall stand in 793 (de.wikipedia Danewerk). 'One gate only, through which wagons and horsemen could be sent out and let in' (Annales regni Francorum 808). Hollingstedt on the Treene, 16 to 18 km west by ox-cart (de.wikipedia Haithabu; Hollingstedt). The complaint about two tolls: story/sayings_793.json say.inv.c.sliesthorp. No toll rate is recorded

sites.name: The king's field
sites.see: A wide heath south of the houses, purple in late summer. When a king is here it is covered: tents of striped wool, horse lines out to the edge of sight, shields hung on spear racks, and in the middle an open space with a high seat carried out of a ship. A spokesman stands in front of it and repeats what is said behind him. Horse sweat, trampled heather, roasting meat, a horn now and then. When no king is here, sheep.
sites.source: Godfred came 'with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom' (Annales regni Francorum 804) and stayed some days in 808. No hall or thing-place has been found (dossier 2): the field and the high seat are the game's own. The English name 'at the Heaths' (Ohthere) gives the heath

sites.name: The grave field
sites.see: Low ground south of the brook, pocked with small mounds and burnt patches, each with a stone or a post. A woman pours ale on one. Further on, two green barrows stand side by side where the old road passes. In later years there is a great mound here with a boat's stem showing through the turf, and by the ford a tall stone cut with runes, painted red in the grooves. Wind in dry grass, a lark, an old smell of fire.
sites.source: Nearly 1,350 burials: Danish cremation pits, chamber graves, Saxon and Slav urns, later Christian graves (ZBSA on Arents and Eisenschmidt 2010; de.wikipedia Haithabu). The boat chamber grave of about 900; the mound pair Twebargen; the four rune stones of about 940 to 1000 (de.wikipedia Bootkammergrab; Runensteine von Haithabu). The ale offering is invented in the period's manner

sites.name: The moneyer's bench
sites.see: A lean-to against a goldsmith's house, open at the front. A man sits astride a block with an iron die set in it, lays a thin round of silver on the die, sets a second die on top and strikes once. The pennies are small and light and say Dorestad in letters that have begun to turn into a ship. A boy counts them into a wooden bowl. The moneyer cannot read them and says so.
sites.source: The first coins of the North, from about 825, copying Dorestad's Frankish pennies (en.wikipedia Hedeby; da.wikipedia Hedebymønter; economy/silver_coin.md). No moneyer is named (dossier 3); the bench is invented

sites.name: The church by the harbour
sites.see: A small church of upright oak planks under a shingle roof, a stone's throw from the jetties, with a priest's house beside it. By the door stands a frame of two posts and a beam: empty at first, then with a bronze bell in it the height of a man's forearm. Inside, a board altar, a cross, one lamp, a row of boys reading from wax tablets. Frisians and Saxons go in. The Danes mending nets outside do not look round.
sites.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar 24, 31-32 (tr. Robinson 1921): the church at the port, the priest's house, the door shut by Count Hovi, the bell. The church has never been found in the ground and its saint is not recorded: none is named. A bronze bell of about 950 was found in the harbour in 1978 (de.wikipedia Glocke von Haithabu). The oak frame is from chain_the_bell

people.name: Asulf
people.trait: A dealer in captives who thinks himself an honest man: feeds his lots, keeps families together when it costs nothing, remembers every sale.
people.want: Frankish blades, which buy more captives than silver does; and a quiet trade.
people.fear: A king who decides the trade is his; sickness in the pen.
people.voice: Says less than he means; names prices in ounces of silver and never haggles twice.
people.looks: Around forty, stout, a plaited beard, a good grey cloak with a silver ring pin, an arm ring he cuts pieces from to pay, a switch of hazel in his hand.
knows: every lot he has bought and where it went: the island boys went east with a Svea, the grown men south by the Saxon road
that the one island boy who could tally came through three summers after the rest, and fetched more than the other three together
what a Frankish blade fetches here, and who buys for a lord with many ships
which ships came in from the west coast and what their summers took
what silver weighs: the ounce and the mark, and whose scales are light
who owes whom on the strand

ties.note: the same person
sells what the king's wars take, and fears the day the king wants the trade for himself
buys what Thorleif brings home each autumn, and pays him in blades when he has them
is owed for a lot Thiadbod took on credit and has not forgotten the sum
Ravn will not sit with him and neither says why
the Svea who takes the young ones east and pays on the day
they sold in the same market and, after 808, in the same harbour
he sold the boy and remembers the price to the grain
she takes his guests' silver before he can; he calls her the second toll
the ferryman carries his lots over the Slie and is paid late, on purpose, every year
paid a debt for one of the host's sons here and has never mentioned it, which Hroald finds worse than being asked
the carter at Ripa took one lot of his over the heath and has refused the work since
the ale-wife in the Vik served him once, saw what he bought across her bench, and will not again
she went through his father's pen as a girl and was bought back by her brother; she has not forgotten, and he has (?)
the king's man under the awning at Reric is the one man in those lanes who drinks with him
bought Saxons of the Wendish riders after the Sventana field on credit of a sort; neither side agrees what is still owed
sells the hall on Zealand its field hands on a tally, and is paid after harvest
the watchman at the hall's landing has twice caught him landing lots by night to save the lord's share
Thorleif's wife will not have him sleep under her roof; he sleeps in his ship and says the air is better
the ale-wife in Skane shut her door on a lot of his; he tells men her ale is thin
the man who speaks for the strand counts heads at his pen each morning, against lots landed by night

lines.greet: You are from the river. I am Asulf. I buy and sell people, and I pay in silver by weight. Sit, if that does not offend you.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the small boat. You came back, so I did not cheat you, or you did not notice. Either is good for trade.
rumour: Blades with the smith's name in them fetch three times their river price here. I pay more. I pay in people, who are worth more further on.
The island lot came at summer's end. Church boys, soft hands. They went east with a Svea. Christians do not sell south; the Franks ask questions.
A king who counts ships will one day count pens. I feed my stock and keep my sticks straight. Let him find a fault in that.
Thorleif of the west coast brings me what his summers take. He wants swords for it. Everybody wants swords. Nobody has asked what I want.
lines.saying: A dead lot pays nobody. That is all the kindness there is in it, and it is more than most men manage.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you find what you say you do not carry, I am here until the first frost.

people.source: invented (spine cast.asulf): a dealer in captives. Hedeby and Birka were markets for people; Anskar bought Danish and Slav boys (Rimbert 15). The name is As- and -ulf, attested Norse parts

people.name: Hallbjorn
people.trait: The ferryman on the Slie: as a young man he sat on the low bench in the king's hall at Hleidr and learned a hundred verses, of which he has kept about six. Knows every shoal and tells nobody for nothing.
people.want: To hear the three wave riddles said together once more before he dies; and a boy with the patience to learn the water.
people.fear: That the old words go into the ground with him and the other bench-fellows, and nobody notices.
people.voice: Slow, sideways; answers a plain question with a harder one. Talks to the water as to a neighbour he has not forgiven.
people.looks: Past fifty, long-armed, white hair in a tail, a face like a dried apple, a tarred hood, bare feet, a small leather bag tied under his seat with tarred cord.
knows: the Slie from the mouth to the inner water: the bar, the broads, the gap in the log fence at the narrows
one of the three riddles of Aegir's daughters, and who has her sisters
who taught Ravn, and what name that man goes by on the rune sticks
who crossed the water this week and in what hurry
where the king's watch sits north of the narrows

ties.note: they sat on one bench at Hleidr when they had hair; he knows Ravn's name and will not say it
his dead brother's wife; he eats at her fire and pays in fish and opinions
carries the dealer's lots over the water and dislikes the fare
the wright tars his boat each spring and is paid in a riddle he never answers
a Vestfold shipman who has the first of the three sisters (?)
a singer among the Svear who has the second (?)
the king's skald at Hleidr sat one bench higher and still corrects him by messenger (?)
the blind reciter at Salhaugar, off whose bench his six verses come; he hands on the old man's sticks
the brew-wife of the hall fed him on the low bench; he still sends her eels

lines.greet: Sit in the middle and keep your feet off the bag. The fare is a cut of silver, or a thing I have not heard before.
lines.greet_again: You. I told the water you would be back. It did not answer, but it never does when it agrees.
rumour: There is a fence of logs across the narrows, older than my father. Kings built it. I know the gap. Strangers find it with their keels.
A grey Northman sails with you. Ask him about the low bench by the door. Then watch him talk about the weather.
I have one of three sisters. A Vestfold shipman has the first, a singer among the Svear the second. White hoods, hard beds. Bring me all three.
A short pull north of the fence the king keeps ships and men on a hill. They watch the mouth. Nobody comes into this water unseen.
lines.saying: In calm weather they make no stir. There. I have said too much already.
lines.farewell: Step out on the shore side. The other side is deeper than it looks, like most things here.

people.source: invented (spine riddle_road hook; chain_riddle_trail s04 leaves him unnamed). The name is Hall- and -bjorn, attested Norse parts. His riddle is Gestumblindi's third wave riddle (riddles_793.json r-gest-23; Vigfusson and Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale 1883). The barrier: de.wikipedia Schlei-Seesperrwerk; the watch at Füsing: de.wikipedia Wikingersiedlung von Füsing

people.name: Gunnhild
people.trait: A widow who keeps the ale-house and answers for her guests before the men of the place: a stranger with no host is driftwood, and she decides who is driftwood.
people.want: Her son Thorgar home from whatever ship he is in this year; malt; and guests who come back.
people.fear: A fleet in the Slie with nothing to eat; fire in the thatch; her tally sticks lost.
people.voice: Brisk and fond. Remembers what every guest drank, owed and said about his wife. Forgets a debt in your favour once and never twice.
people.looks: About forty, broad, strong forearms, hair under a linen cloth, a brown strap-dress with two bronze brooches and a string of glass beads between them, keys and a knife at her belt.
knows: who is in harbour, where from, and who answers for them
the price of ale, bread and fodder this week, and why
which Saxons live among the Danes and what they are afraid of
who is hiring crew and who should not be sailed with
what Asulf paid for what, because his men drink here

ties.note: her husband's brother; she feeds him and he pretends it is a favour to her
she warns guests off his credit and takes his men's silver every night
the wright built her husband's last boat and still eats at her table on the strength of it
she lodges Saxons who would not be moved, and a Saxon aboard is welcome for their sake
after 808 she stood host for his household the first winter, and he has not let her pay for wax since
a sister married west to Ripa, who sends word with the carters (?)
Thiadbod's crew left three sticks unpaid; she will tell anyone
the man who speaks for the strand takes her word on a stranger; she takes his on a king
the Wend's wife, whose household she stood host for in the first winter after 808; they have six words in common and use them all

lines.greet: Ale is brewed, the bench is dry, the fire is yours until you fall asleep at it. I am Gunnhild. Who answers for you here?
lines.greet_again: I kept your stick. Three notches unpaid, or two. I forget in your favour once and never twice.
rumour: A man with no host here is driftwood. Anyone may pick him up. Say you lodge with me and they will leave you be.
There are Saxons in my back room who would not be moved into Francia. They pay in work. They jump when a horse passes.
Asulf pays what he owes on the day, which is why nobody likes owing him. Do not take his credit. Take mine.
The ferryman is my husband's brother. He will ask you a riddle. Answer wrongly with confidence; he respects it.
lines.saying: The beer was all drunk or not yet brewed, the verse says. Here it is always one or the other, and I decide which.
lines.farewell: Go with a full skin. Come back before the stick rots.

people.source: invented. The name is Gunn- and -hild, attested Norse parts. A host answers for a guest: npc_text_encounters.md 1.1 (the host) and chain_saxon_exiles_804 s06. Her verse is Hávamál 66 (tr. Bellows 1923): 'The beer was all drunk, or not yet brewed'

people.name: Thormund
people.trait: The wright on the slip: builds by eye from split oak and has an opinion of every hull in the harbour, most of them low. Honest about what a boat will not do.
people.want: Good green oak, iron for rivets, and one order in his life for a ship long enough to be remembered.
people.fear: A king's levy that takes his oak and his boys for warships and pays in thanks.
people.voice: Speaks to the boat first and the owner second. Short, flat, unkind in a friendly way.
people.looks: Mid-thirties, thick shoulders, sandy beard full of chips, a leather apron black with tar, a broad axe in his hand and a spoon auger in his belt.
knows: what your hull needs and what it will cost in days
which boats on the strand are for sale and what is wrong with each
how the Wends peg a boat and the Frisians build a tub
where oak, tar and iron come from this year and at what price
when to order: before leaf-fall for first open water

ties.note: tars the ferry each spring for a riddle he has never answered
eats at her table more than he pays for
in 804 and 808 the king's ships come first on his slip, whether he likes it or not
the wright at Ahus; each says the other builds for fair weather (?)
called Thiadbod's big ship a floating barn within Thiadbod's hearing
the Gutes' wright says he builds long and narrow for kings; Thormund says Gotland boats are tubs for sheep; each has mended the other's work

lines.greet: Do not lean on her, the tar is wet. I am Thormund. I build what the oak allows, and I mend what other men built.
lines.greet_again: Let me see what you did to her. Hm. The sea did half of it. The other half was you.
rumour: Oak comes down from the north shore, split, never sawn. A split plank bends. A sawn one sulks and then breaks.
The Wends peg their boats with wood where we rivet with iron. They float. I looked for the trick and it is only patience.
A Frisian hull is a tub. I say it kindly. She carries twice what mine does, and arrives when the weather has finished with her.
Order before the leaves fall and she swims at first open water. Order in spring and you get my opinion of spring orders.
lines.saying: From the ship seek swiftness. The rest of that verse is about women, and you may ask Gunnhild.
lines.farewell: Bring her back whole. If you cannot, bring back the rivets.

people.source: invented. The name is Thor- and -mund, attested Norse parts. Boat-builders at Hedeby (haithabu-danewerk.de); Slav boats pegged with treenails (ship_classes_793.json baltic_coastal_boat). His verse is Hávamál 82 (tr. Bellows 1923): 'From the ship seek swiftness, from the shield protection'

people.name: Godfred
people.trait: Proud and exact: counts his ships against the emperor's and builds a wall across a neck of land. Met here only in the summers of 804 and 808, in the open, among armed men.
people.want: The toll of every ship between the two seas; Frisia and Saxony as his own provinces.
people.fear: Nothing he would name. He should have feared his own following.
people.voice: Short and public; never alone. He speaks to merchants through a spokesman, who says 'the king says' and looks at nobody.
people.looks: In his forties, tall, long fair hair combed back, a red cloak with a great gilt pin, gold arm rings, a sword with a silvered hilt; always among armed men, horses and ships.
knows: how many ships and horsemen he has, to the last
what Reric paid in toll, and why it now pays here
where the wall will run and who owes days on it
what the emperor wants, and how long the emperor can be made to wait

ties.note: the same person
the Obodrite prince and the emperor's ally; Godfred's men kill him at Reric in 809
one of the merchants he carried off; the king does not know his name
the dealer sells what the king's wars take and is paid in the king's notice, which he would rather not have
his son, a young man in 810
the man who speaks for the strand, whom he makes keeper of the one gate in 808
his man under the awning at Reric, who weighs the due and has never yet been told he does it well
the steward who speaks for him to merchants at the hall on Zealand
a chief of the Vik who sends a gift each year and hopes it is taken for obedience

lines.greet: The king sees you. He asks what ship, whose man, and what the emperor's horsemen eat this year. Answer the last one carefully.
lines.greet_again: The king remembers the small boat from the river. He remembers everything that floats. He has counted most of it.
rumour: The emperor waits beyond the river for the king to come to him. The king has come exactly this far. He finds the view sufficient.
Reric paid the king good toll, so the king has brought Reric here, where the toll is nearer. The merchants will come to see the sense.
There will be a wall from the eastern water to the western sea, and one gate in it. Carts and riders pass there. So will you.
The king says Frisia and Saxony are his own provinces, and that he will visit the emperor at home shortly. He has the ships.
lines.saying: A king who rides to another king's hall has already paid. So the king says. I only carry it.
lines.farewell: You may trade. The king's peace lies on the strand as far as the brook. Past the brook it is your own.

people.source: Annales regni Francorum 804, 808, 810: at Sliesthorp with fleet and horse in 804, by ship with Reric's merchants in 808, killed by a follower in 810. His birth year is a guess (?). The boast about Frisia, Saxony and the emperor's own hall is Einhard, Life of Charles 14 (tr. Grant 1907), not opened tonight (?). The spokesman and all the words are invented

people.name: Horik
people.trait: Godfred's son, who learned what his father's pride cost: disowns the fleets that burn Dorestad, takes the bishop's gifts, lets a church be built and stays unbaptised.
people.want: The emperor's friendship on his own terms; Frisia, if it is offered.
people.voice: Guarded; answers a question with a gift. Lets a silence do the work his father gave to a spokesman.
people.looks: Grey, heavy, a king's red cloak and gold arm rings, a bench with shields behind him, a bishop's gift of Frankish glass on the board in front of him.
knows: whose the fleets on the Rhine are, whatever he says
what leave the bishop has, and that he can take it back
which of his kin want a share of the kingdom
what the emperor's envoys were told last, word for word

ties.note: the same person
his father, whose wall he keeps and whose manners he does not
takes the bishop's gifts, gives him a roof at the port, and is never baptised
a kinsman with a Frankish river and an eye on a Danish kingdom
the hall's skald on Zealand makes his verses for Godfred's son and is paid in rings (?)
the keeper of the Svear's town counts Horik's ships and exiles as its nearest danger
a boy of his kin and his name, the one left to be king after the war of 854

lines.greet: You are from Dorestad. Then you have come to ask me about ships. Sit. Take this cup; it is Frankish, like the question.
lines.greet_again: The merchant from the river. My father would have counted your boat. I count your friends. It is cheaper.
rumour: Those fleets were not mine. I took their chiefs and hanged them, and I have told the emperor so. He might thank me with Frisia.
The bishop asks for a roof and a priest by the harbour. Merchants from your river like it. I have said yes to the roof.
My brother's sons want a share of the kingdom. I gave them a little. A little is how it begins.
The bishop brings gifts and asks for nothing the first day. I have learned from him. Have you eaten?
lines.saying: My father built a wall, and one of his own men killed him behind it. Walls are for the outside.
lines.farewell: Go in my peace. If anyone on the strand doubts it, show him the cup.

people.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar 24, 31 (tr. Robinson 1921): he allowed the church and was killed in 854. Sole king from about 828 (en.wikipedia Horik I). That he disowned the fleets, hanged their chiefs and asked for Frisia: Annales Bertiniani 836, 838, as in the spine (not opened tonight) (?). His birth year is a guess, and that a merchant met him at this port and not at a hall elsewhere is the game's choice (?). The words are invented

people.name: Anskar
people.trait: A visionary and a stubborn one: buys boys out of slavery to make them priests, gives gifts before he asks, travels in merchants' ships.
people.want: A church and a bell at Sliaswic, a priest at Birka, and the leave of kings who can take it back.
people.fear: That the work will die with him.
people.voice: Soft and patient; never argues with a king in public. Counts ships, boys and books, in that order.
people.looks: As first met, twenty-five, thin, tonsured, a monk's black habit worn at the hem, barefoot in the boat; later a greying archbishop in a hair shirt under a plain cloak.
knows: which merchants here were baptised at Dorstadt or Hamburg, and which only took the sign of the cross
what a psalter is worth, and that someone in the north has thirty-nine of his books
which boys in the pens can be bought, and for how much
what the king has allowed this year, and what the count thinks of it
who sails for Birka and whether he can be trusted with a priest

ties.note: the same person
the king whose leave he lives on; he brings gifts and never presses
the prefect of Birka, baptised by his hand in 829 (?)
the daughter of Frideburg of his flock at Birka, who carries her mother's alms to Dorstadt
an Englishman among the Svear who still holds a stick like a pen; the bishop would like to know his name
the priest for the second church, at Ripa, comes from his school (?)
travels under the count's peace when he goes by the Rhine mouth
the boy king who lets the count shut the church, then puts the count out and allows the bell
a Frisian in the Vik who sends word by any ship and asks only when a priest might come

lines.greet: God keep you. You came by ship, so you have news and wet feet. Sit by the door; the Danes like to see who is inside.
lines.greet_again: You again, thank God. I count the ships that come back. It is a shorter list than the ones I bless.
rumour: Many here were baptised at Dorstadt or Hamburg and hid it. Now they hear Mass openly. Others take the sign of the cross and wait for their deathbed.
I set out for the Svear with nearly forty books. Sea robbers took the ship and I arrived on foot with none. Someone has them. Books are not eaten.
I buy boys out of the pens here, Danes and Wends, and teach them letters. The dealer thinks I am a poor judge of stock.
The count nailed our door shut and said the gods were angry. The young king put the count out. Now he allows a bell. Pray it holds.
lines.saying: A king's leave is a loan. I spend it the day I get it.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and bring me a psalter if you see one for sale among the combs.

people.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar 7, 10, 15, 24, 31-32 (tr. Robinson 1921): north with Harald in 826; robbed of nearly forty books on the way to Birka; buying boys; the church at Sliaswic; the shut door and the bell. Born 8 September 801, died 3 February 865. That his first school stood at this port is the spine's reading, not Rimbert's (?). The words are invented

people.name: Wulfstan
people.trait: A seaman with an eye for other people's customs: the Ests' drinking, their kings, the horse-race for a dead man's goods, the cold they can make in summer.
people.want: Amber and a fair wind home; and somebody who has been east to tell him he has it right before he tells his king.
people.fear: Not recorded. (Ours: getting the order of the islands wrong in front of King Alfred.)
people.voice: Lists the lands to port and to starboard like a rope of knots. Exact about days, vague about himself.
people.looks: Around forty, a sea cloak, a trimmed beard, an English knife with an inlaid blade, a string of rough amber round his wrist.
knows: the run to Truso: seven days and nights under sail, and what lies on either hand
the Ests: their forts and kings, their honey, mares' milk and mead, and how they bury
what amber costs at the lake and what it fetches here
which Northman came five days from Sciringes heal with walrus teeth
what an English king will pay to be told the shape of the world

ties.note: the same person
they drank together on the jetty and each counted the other's days
the amber-cutter at the Ests' lake let him have his amber on a promise to come back with English cloth (?)
sails out of the English king's ports and tells his voyages at court (?)
the same person, as he is met among the Ests
bought a pair of brooches for his wife from the town goldsmith, and paid in an hour's talk of the Ests besides
a woman selling from a chest lid at a river mouth in Skane, who answered every question he put

lines.greet: English? No, Frisian; I hear it now. Wulfstan. Sit, and tell me if you have been east. I have, and nobody believes me.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. Good. I have remembered two more islands since we spoke, and both lie to port.
rumour: From here to Truso, seven days and nights, under sail the whole way. Wendland to starboard. Langaland, Laland, Falster and Scania to port.
Among the Ests a dead man lies in his house a month or two, and they drink until he is burned. They can make cold. I saw it.
They lay the dead man's goods in heaps along a road, the biggest furthest off, and ride for them. So fast horses are dear there.
A Northman called Ohthere came here from Sciringes heal in five days. He says the English lived in these lands once. They are flat enough.
lines.saying: Say which hand the land was on. Everything else a man tells you about a voyage is weather.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. If you go east, count the days yourself. Then come and tell me I was right.

people.source: Wulfstan's voyage in Alfred's Orosius, about 890 (Hakluyt, The Discovery of Muscovy, Cassell 1893; texts_793.json wulfstan, ohthere). Nothing is known of him but the voyage: his age, his years here and his words are the game's (?)

people.name: Gunulf
people.trait: The man who speaks for the strand: a householder with the longest memory of who landed what, made keeper of the king's one gate in 808 because nobody else could count carts.
people.want: The landing gift given without argument, and to hand the tally stick to a son, not to a king's stranger.
people.fear: A king who comes in person; and, after 808, a cart he let through that he should not have.
people.voice: Flat and patient. States what is usual, never what is owed. Counts under his breath while you talk.
people.looks: Mid forties, spare, grey-fair hair cut at the jaw, a faded green cloak with a bronze ring pin, a long tally stick in his belt and a knotted measuring cord over one shoulder.
knows: every keel in the inner water, whose guest she is, and what she gave
what the gate takes on a cart for the western river, from 808
what comes over each autumn from the king's awning at Reric, to the ounce
who owes days on the wall and who has paid them
which way the king's mind is turning, a week before the strand knows

ties.note: takes the autumn's due from the awning at Reric and counts it without comment, which Skardi takes for praise
from 804 the king's man in fact; from 808 the keeper of the one gate
takes her word on a stranger; she takes his on a king
the dealer lands lots by night to save the gift; Gunulf counts heads at the pen in the morning
sends the strand's takings on to the steward of the hall on Zealand each winter (?)
paced out the Wend's plot with his own cord in 808, and has not yet been given the gift that is usual

lines.greet: You lie where the brook has cut the sand, like everyone. I speak for this strand until somebody greater says he does. A gift is usual.
lines.greet_again: The small boat from the river. Your stake hole is still in the shallows. Nobody used it. I would have heard.
rumour: Nobody takes a toll here. A gift is given to the man who speaks for the place. I am told the difference is important.
The due from the Wends' market comes over each autumn under a Dane's seal. It grows every year. So does the king's interest in it.
There is a wall now, and one gate, and I am the man with the stick. I did not ask for the stick.
lines.saying: A gift is a toll that was asked for politely.
lines.farewell: Go out on the land wind. Leave your stake. I will know it.

people.source: invented: the spokesman of the place to whom a landing gift is given (Design/content/lore/law_tolls.md 11: no toll is recorded), and from 808 the king's man at the one gate (Annales regni Francorum 808; the gate site of this file). He is the 'king's man at the Schlei' of reric.skardi's tie. The first named warden of the border is Gluomi, in 817 (Annales regni Francorum 817). The name is Gunulf (DR 230)

people.name: Tofi
people.trait: A comb-maker of the pit-houses who sells to five peoples and trusts none of their scales but his own.
people.want: Shed antler by the boatload, reindeer if it can be had, and one summer without the Skane men at the next hut.
people.fear: A cough that will not go: the dust gets into a man.
people.voice: Runs down the buyer's judgement before the buyer has opened his mouth, then gives fair measure.
people.looks: About thirty-five, narrow-shouldered, white dust to the elbows, a fine-toothed saw in his hand and three combs thrust in his belt like knives.
knows: what antler fetches by the bundle, red deer and reindeer
which of the summer craftsmen are from the river mouth in Skane, and what they charge
what the Svear pay for a comb with a case
who in the pit-houses stretches his bronze with lead

ties.note: the Skane comb-maker sets up beside him each summer; they watch each other's prices and borrow each other's saws
three notches on a stick over her vat, which she has not forgotten in his favour
sells the dealer combs for his lots, so that they look worth more, and dislikes the reason
the Svea buys his cased combs for the east and counts the teeth

lines.greet: Antler? No. Then you want combs, and I am the wrong man to ask about the price, because I made them.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. Your last dozen: did the teeth hold? They hold. I ask because I like to hear it.
rumour: A Svea wants combs with a case. A comb in a case is two combs' work. He says one and a half. We are still talking.
The Skane men come at the first day of summer and go home with the herring. In between I sell at their price or not at all.
Reindeer antler comes off the north-way boats. It saws cleaner than red deer. Nobody here has seen the beast.
lines.saying: A comb has many teeth and one back. So has a market.
lines.farewell: Mind the floor going out. It is white to the ankle, and all of it was money once.

people.source: invented: the comb-makers shown by over 340,000 pieces of waste at Hedeby (en.wikipedia Hedeby; de.wikipedia Haithabu), and the rival of ahus.toke's tie; the summer craftsmen from Ahus are Callmer 2002. Reindeer antler in the combs of the Danish markets: Ashby, Coutu and Sindbaek 2015 (not opened) (?). The name is Tofi (names_placeholder.json)

people.name: Urm
people.trait: A town goldsmith of the busy years: casts brooches by the hundred from one model, gilds with quicksilver, and sees no shame in either.
people.want: All the quicksilver that comes north, so that his gilding is the only gilding; and a boy who does not cough.
people.fear: His hands, which have begun to shake; a hall smith with one perfect piece.
people.voice: Brisk, a seller's voice. Names a price by the dozen and looks past you for the next buyer.
people.looks: About forty, quick, a singed fair beard, stained fingers that tremble a little, a leather apron, a tray of identical brooches on a strap round his neck.
knows: what quicksilver costs and who has it
which brooch pattern sells this summer from the Slie to the Svear's lake
true silver from plated, by the knife
what the hall smith on Zealand calls his work, and what he calls the hall smith

ties.note: the hall smith on Zealand makes one thing in a winter; Urm makes a hundred and says so
of the families that came from the river mouth in Skane when the town there was given up; his moulds were his grandfather's (?)
sold the English skipper a pair of brooches for his wife and heard about the Ests for an hour

lines.greet: Brooches. A pair for a wife, a dozen for a crew to take home. All the same, all sound. Which?
lines.greet_again: You again. The last pair held their pins? Then you want a dozen.
rumour: The hall smith on Zealand makes one thing in a winter and will not say what it is. I make a hundred and say so. We both eat.
Quicksilver comes north in sealed horn, by few hands. I buy all of it. It is not greed. It is so that the work is even.
My boy coughs and his hands shake. He is young for it. Mine only began at forty.
lines.saying: One good model is worth ten good ideas.
lines.farewell: Come back when the pin breaks. It will not break.

people.source: invented: the town goldsmiths whose fire-gilding left mercury in the workshops (en.wikipedia Hedeby; de.wikipedia Haithabu), and the rival of hleidr.soti in the story hleidr.chair_and_birds. Brooches cast in series from one model are the finds' own; the family from Ahus is the story ahus.fences, ending 'to_the_slie'. The name is Urm (Annales regni Francorum 811, one of the twelve Danes who swore the peace: a common name, not that man)

people.name: Godwine
people.trait: An English moneyer who left a bench at home, where the king calls the coin in every six winters and fines a light penny, for a bench where nobody has ever seen a fine. Cuts his own dies, weighs first, counts second, and believes the first.
people.want: Old silver for the pot: arm rings, cut coin, a hall's cups; English pennies, which need no testing; and ale brewed as it is at home.
people.fear: A king who learns what a fine is, or one who wants the pennies lighter and the count the same.
people.voice: Slow Danish with an English mouth, and the hammer's pauses in it. Speaks of silver as other men speak of weather.
people.looks: A man of forty with thick wrists, a leather cap, a short apron scorched at the hem, an iron die in one hand and a hammer in the other, a small scale on a nail behind him.
knows: what a penny of this bench weighs, and what the king says it weighs
what old vessels and rings fetch for the pot, less his tenth
which pennies from England are good, by king, and how often that king calls them in
who has brought a hall's silver to be melted, and from where

ties.note: the old steward on Zealand will take his pennies only by weight, and tells his men why
the priest across the water from the old hall wanted the same four cups for his altar that the moneyer wanted for his fire

lines.greet: Silver in, pennies out, less my tenth. The letters say the king's name and mine. Weigh them if you doubt either of us.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Your last silver made forty pennies and a little dust. I kept the dust. That is the custom, here and at home.
rumour: The pennies they struck here before me had a town's name on them, a town far to the south that nobody has seen in a hundred years, copied until no one could read it. Mine can be read. That is what I was sent for.
English pennies come home in sacks. I weigh them, and then I count them, and both come out the same. At home that is the law. Here it is new.
An old steward on Zealand takes coin only by weight. He is right, and he is the last.
lines.saying: A penny is a promise. A weight is a fact.
lines.farewell: Go well. Bring rings, not promises.

people.source: The same man as the moneyer of harbour.chain_maldon_991.s07_pennies_north, made a person here so that the bench has one man and not two. King Swein's penny of about 995 copies King Aethelred's and names a moneyer Godwine among the Danes (?): the name is real, the man is the game's. Where that penny was struck is not known; that it was at the Slie is the chain's choice (?), and that he came north as early as 985 is invented, so that the story hleidr.pot_under_the_floor (from 988) has its moneyer. The older pennies of the place copy Dorestad's long after Dorestad is gone (da.wikipedia Hedebymonter; Design/content/realms/denmark.md); English pennies from 991. The rival of hleidr.alli in the story hleidr.pot_under_the_floor

people.name: Hored
people.trait: A bishop named for a town he has hardly seen: careful, landless, and aware that his see is a line in a synod's record.
people.want: A church at the port that is open more winters than it is shut, and a king's baptism to stand behind it.
people.fear: To be the bishop of a parchment.
people.voice: A Saxon's Danish, slow. Says 'if God wills and the king allows', and means the second half.
people.looks: Around forty, a plain dark cloak over a linen alb, a short staff, a travelling altar in a satchel, the look of a man counting a congregation and getting a small number.
knows: what was done at Ingelheim in 948, and who stood beside him
what Archbishop Adaldag wants of the three new sees
which merchants of the port are baptised and which only signed with the cross
whether the church by the harbour has its roof this year

ties.note: made bishop for the Danes with him on one day at Ingelheim
a hundred years dead: Hored holds the church the old bishop begged a king for

lines.greet: God keep you. I am bishop of this place. It was said so at Ingelheim, before the king and the pope's legate. Here it is said less often.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. You have been to Ripa? Then tell me how Leofdag does. We were made on one day, like twins, and have about one church between us.
rumour: Three of us were made bishops for the Danes on one day: Sliaswic, Ripa, Aarhus. The archbishop was pleased. The Danes were not asked.
There are Christians at this port from your river, from Saxony, from England. They hear Mass when there is a priest and a roof. Both are seasonal.
The king over the Danes lets us be. His son listens. I am told that is how it begins.
lines.saying: Anskar begged a roof of one king and a bell of the next. I have both, and the nerve of neither.
lines.farewell: Go with God. If you see Bremen, say Sliaswic has a bishop. If you see Sliaswic's bishop, say the same to him.

people.source: Real: Hored, named bishop of Sliaswic at the synod of Ingelheim, 7 June 948, with Liafdag of Ripa and Reginbrand of Aarhus (Adam of Bremen ii.4; chronicle_793.json 948-danish-bishops; de.wikipedia Hored; Liste der Bischofe von Schleswig). Whether he ever came to the port is not known: that a merchant meets him here is the game's (?). His people, his years after 948, his looks and every word are invented (?)

people.name: Horik the younger
people.trait: A boy made king after the kinsmen's war of 854: first led by the men who shut the church, then his own master, who put the count out, opened the door and allowed a bell.
people.want: To be king in fact; and the friendship of the Franks' kings and their bishop, on terms his great men can stomach.
people.fear: The great men who made him; and the exiles of the royal kin, with their fleets and their Frankish rivers.
people.voice: Young, formal, a little too loud. Listens to the man on his right before he answers.
people.looks: About fourteen when made king, about seventeen when he gives ground at Ripa: slight, fair, a king's red cloak cut down to fit and gold rings too big for his arms, older men standing close.
knows: who nailed the church door shut, and why he let them
what the bishop asked and what he gave: a bell here, a plot at Ripa
which of the exiles of his kin holds which Frankish river
what the pope wrote to him, as it was read out

ties.note: of his kin and his name; king after him, when almost all the kin were dead
puts out the count who shut the church, asks the bishop's priest back, and allows the bell
gave the ground the priest stands on at Ripa, and leave for him to live there
the exile with the Frankish river comes home to try for his kingdom, and goes back

lines.greet: You are from the Franks' river. The bishop has spoken of your people. Stand there. Burghard, what does he want?
lines.greet_again: The merchant from Dorestad. I know you. I am told I know you.
rumour: Hovi said the gods were angry at the strange god, and I let him shut the door. I was a boy. I am not, now. Hovi is elsewhere.
The bishop asked for a bell. My kinsman's men say a bell is unlawful. I asked whose law. Nobody could tell me.
I have given the bishop ground at Ripa for a second church. Burghard asked it, who is kin to me and to the king before me.
lines.saying: They made me king because I was the one left. I am learning the rest.
lines.farewell: Go in my peace. It is newer than my kinsman's, and I mean it to last longer.

people.source: Real: Horik the younger, made king in 854 after Horik and almost all the royal kin were killed. Hovi, count of the port, shut the church; the king put him out, asked the priest back, allowed a bell, and gave a plot for a church at Ripa, Burghard speaking for the bishop (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 31-32, tr. Robinson 1921). Pope Nicholas I wrote to him in 864, after which he is not heard of (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horik_II). Rorik's attempt on the kingdom in 855 to 857: Annales Fuldenses 857, as in the spine (?). His age, his looks and every word are invented (?). The young king of ripa.priest's tie

stories.title: A man who remembers every sale
stories.summary: The boys carried off from the holy island in June 793 came through Asulf's pen at summer's end, and Asulf forgets no lot: he knows they went east with a Svea, because Christians cannot be sold south to the Franks. He will say so to a man he has reason to oblige, and what the merchant gives him for it, blades, a favour or nothing, decides what kind of friend the house has at Sliesthorp.
stories.picture: The fenced pen at dusk: a stout man in a grey cloak holding a notched stick up to the last light, a row of sticks on a peg behind him, and on a bench a bell without a tongue.

beats.text: The bishop's people give the names of the boys who were taken and what will be paid for each. One was an oblate of twelve with a fair hand, Tidwine.

Asulf has watched your boat since she touched the strand. Ask about the island lot and he takes down a stick and counts the notches: church boys, soft hands, sold at summer's end. Where they went has a price, and he names it once.

Among the odd things on his bench lies a block of calfskins with the covers torn off. A Svea is counting its leaves to scrape them for tallies. Asulf was told to ask more than skins are worth, and to ask you.
Gunnhild heard it from Asulf's own men over her ale: the Svea is Holmfast of Birka, who weighs everything three times. She tells you for nothing, because Asulf would have charged.
Holmfast keeps an Englishman who can tally and read marks, and does not think of selling him. The man answers in Norse with an English turn, and holds the tally stick like a pen.

Thorleif's hall, where the lot came from: English boys herd the swine (two until the summer of 796, when the one who can tally is sold east; one after), and a woman wears a brooch that was a book mount. He sells for silver by weight or a sword, never for prayers.
At the Vik's market the ale-wife saw it begin: three English boys sold to Asulf on the strand in the autumn of 793, and a fourth, who could count, kept by the crew that took him.
Asulf's tally stick is put into Thorleif's hand by a Frisian. Thorleif reads the notches, laughs first, and says the dealer could have sent a Dane.

endings.how: Paid Asulf's price in Frankish blades.
endings.text: Asulf tells all of it, exactly, and from then on he is your buyer: he pays in silver or in people and takes every blade you can bring. Ravn does not speak to you for a week. The king's men in the west have one more reason to know your name.
endings.reward: The trail (flag lf_trail_north) and a standing buyer (flag sw_buyer_known); Asulf friendly; Ravn's feeling falls.

endings.how: Did Asulf an honest service first: carried his message to Thorleif, or brought him word of sickness on the road before it reached his pen.
endings.text: He tells it as one tradesman to another and adds what he would not have sold: which boy was clever, and that the Svea who took him does not beat his people. He never mentions it again.
endings.reward: The trail (flag lf_trail_north), the name of Holmfast, and Asulf's word for you with the Svear: one haggle at Birka is 'likely' where it was 'doubtful'.

endings.how: Would not deal with him, and had it from Gunnhild.
endings.text: You have the name and the road without having sat on Asulf's bench. He knows who told you. He is polite about it for the rest of his life, and his credit is never offered to you again.
endings.reward: The trail (flag lf_trail_north); Gunnhild friendly; Ravn's feeling rises; Asulf cool.

stories.reward: The road east to the last boy of Lindisfarne, and one of three kinds of friend at Sliesthorp.

stories.title: One gate
stories.summary: In 804 the king lies here with his fleet and every horseman of his kingdom and will not cross a river to meet the emperor; in 808 he sets the merchants of Reric down on the strand and orders a wall from sea to sea with one gate in it. A merchant who is in harbour those summers can be the king's guest with a plot and days owed on the wall, or the friend of a Wend who wants word of his kin, and not easily both.
stories.picture: A raw earth bank running to the horizon with men and spades along it, a single timber gate with one ox-cart in it, and in front a family sitting on bundles beside a hazel rod driven into the sand.

beats.text: The Slie is full of ships and the heath of horses. Fodder, ale and bread are three times dear, and Gunnhild's vat is empty by noon. The king's spokesman asks every skipper from the west what the emperor's horsemen eat this year.
Dragomir the Wend keeps a wax booth under Thrasco's peace and pays his toll to the Danes' king. A service done him here is remembered on another shore.

The king's men pace out plots with a knotted rope, four rods by eight, short end to the water. The people of Reric sit on what they carried and wait to be told which hazel rods are theirs. Dragomir asks, through a boy, whether any ship goes back along that coast.

A line of men with spades runs west out of sight. Every leader has his length to build, and every guest of the king owes days on it, or the price of a man's days. The king's man at the gate has a stick with your notch on it already.

The ships have gone west, two hundred of them, and Gunnhild's son Thorgar in one. Then a rider: the king is dead, and by one of his own. Nobody on the bench says a name. Hallbjorn says the water knew.
Twelve Danes and twelve Franks have sworn on the Eider, each after his own custom. The gate stays where it is, and so does the man beside it.
For a house that carries malt or rye that summer: the king's buyer and the ale-wife reach the boat at the same moment, and both pay three times the price.
Dragomir sits on a bundle beside four hazel rods with bread on a cloth, and asks every ship whether she goes back along the Wendish coast. He has a tally for his wife's brother.
On the river bank in Skane a Wend in a pegged boat knows Dragomir's cutting, and carries the tally home for nothing. (Sets gf_reric_friend.)

endings.how: Took a plot from the king's man in 808, built on it before the frost, and gave the days owed on the wall.
endings.text: The house has a fenced plot by the brook with its short end to the water, and a notch on the gate-man's stick that means pass. The Wends on the next plot nod and do not visit.
endings.reward: A plot at Sliesthorp (flag unlock_plot_sliesthorp) at 300 d; the gate toll one step lighter while Godfred's line holds the gate; Dragomir cool.

endings.how: Carried Dragomir's word to his kin on the Wendish shore, or did him a service at Reric before it burned.
endings.text: Dragomir stops speaking through the boy. He swears nothing, and says why, and then he feeds you for two days. What comes west from the Wends, wax, honey and furs, comes to your boat first.
endings.reward: Flag gf_reric_friend; first refusal of Wendish wax, honey and furs here at a fair price; a tie that an heir inherits at half strength.

endings.how: Stayed out of the king's sight in 804 and 808 and took neither plot nor errand.
endings.text: Nobody at the gate knows your notch, and you pay like any stranger. But in the west nobody can say you built the Danes' wall, and in 810, when the fleet is off the islands, that is worth something.
endings.reward: No plot before 811; no mark against the house with the Franks; the Frisian ports believe your warning in 810 (helps flag gf_warned).

stories.reward: A place in Godfred's market, a Wendish friend, or clean hands in the west.

stories.title: One of three sisters
stories.summary: The ferryman on the Slie has one of the three riddles of Aegir's daughters; a Vestfold skipper at Skiringssal and a skald at Birka have her sisters. The men who give them all sat on one bench with Ravn, and a merchant who brings the three together learns who has been passing riddles to his house, and why.
stories.picture: A tarred ferry boat alone on grey water, an old man resting on his oars with his mouth open mid-word, and behind him three lines of small white-capped waves coming in one after another.

beats.text: Hallbjorn pushes the fare back across the thwart and asks for a word in place of it. He gives the riddle of the brides who walk over the reefs, and makes the crossing as long as he chooses.
A Vestfold skipper has the first sister: the maids who go weeping to the joy of their father. He gives her for news, and asks whether the old man on the Slie still has his hair.
A skald of the Svear sells the second, the many who go together and have no husbands, for silver. He counts the silver twice.
Say the three together in the boat and Hallbjorn stops rowing. He tells you about the low bench by the door at Hleidr, the man who calls himself Gest, and the grey Northman who sat at the end of it.
The hall where the bench stands. The king's skald sells the hard ones here, and it is here that Ravn was set the question he could not answer.

endings.how: Answered the ferryman's riddle and brought back her two sisters, said together.
endings.text: Hallbjorn unties the bag from under his seat and puts it in your hand without looking at it. He says who paid for your crossings all these years. Ravn, told of it, looks at the water for a long time and then gives you the next riddle.
endings.reward: Flag rd_setter_known; the ferryman's bag (about 60 d of cut silver); the Slie taught by him over one winter (the unlock 'The Slie'); Ravn's trust rises.

endings.how: Answered the one riddle and never fetched the others.
endings.text: He nods, takes his fare in news from then on, and tells you nothing about benches. Each year he asks whether you have been north or east, and each year he seems less sure he will hear the three again.
endings.reward: Free crossings for the house; the riddle solved in the chest; his rumours a week fresher than the market's.

endings.how: Had the answer from somebody else and said it as your own.
endings.text: He hears it in the first three words. He rows you across in silence, takes full fare in silver, and tells Gunnhild, who tells everyone. Nothing worse happens. It is enough.
endings.reward: The riddle counts as solved; no bag, no teaching; the ferryman cool for six years.

stories.reward: Who the riddle-setters are, the ferryman's bag, and the Slie by heart.

stories.title: The back room
stories.summary: Saxons who would not be moved into Francia live among the Danes, and some of them live behind the hanging in Gunnhild's house, paying in work and jumping when a horse passes. A man with no host is a thing found on the beach, so when a Frisian boat lands another family of them somebody has to answer for them: a good deed to a Dane, a crime to a Frank.
stories.picture: The inside of a long house by firelight: a hanging pulled half aside, five people sitting close together on a bench behind it with their bundles still tied, and a broad woman standing in the gap with her arms folded, facing an old man with a staff.

beats.text: There is a back room behind a hanging, and the people in it speak Saxon low. Gunnhild says they would not be moved into Francia, that they pay in work, and that it is no business of anybody from the river. Then she asks whether you have a Saxon aboard.
On a Frisian strand a Saxon asks passage north for himself and four more, out of the king's reach. He has no silver, only a name: a brother with a hearth among the Danes.
You bring them up from the strand. An old Dane with a staff has followed to ask who answers for them here. Gunnhild looks at you first.

The emperor is carrying the Saxons beyond the Elbe into Francia, wives and children and all, and giving their land to the Obodrites. The king's spokesman would like to know how many came north, and in whose boat.
The count's steward has a list of ships that were north of the Eider. Whether yours is on it depends on who was watching the strand, and who you paid.
On the Wends' shore the riders sell what they took on the Sventana field. A smith's son on the rope does not ask to be bought; he asks which way the Danes' country lies.
The Saxon bought at Reric stands on the strand with his hands open. Gunnhild comes down from her door to ask who answers for him. (Sets sx_carried_fugitive.)

endings.how: Answered for them yourself before the old man with the staff, and paid their first winter.
endings.text: They are your guests, and so their conduct is yours. They build a hut on the edge of the houses and the father carts for the Treene road. Every time you land, a Saxon child you do not know brings you bread.
endings.reward: Flag sx_carried_fugitive stands; Gunnhild a fast friend; Brunger's heart rises; a carter on the Treene road at the Saxons' price for the house; a mark with the count's men if it is heard in the west.

endings.how: Let Gunnhild answer for them, and paid her in malt.
endings.text: They go behind the hanging with the others. Gunnhild cuts a new stick with five notches and hangs it over the vat with your name on the end of it. She does not mean you to pay it. She means you to come back.
endings.reward: Gunnhild friendly; free lodging in her house for the crew; the back room's news of Saxony, a season old but true.

endings.how: Set them ashore and sailed, or never carried them.
endings.text: Someone picked them up. A man with no host is driftwood, and there is always a use for driftwood. The back room goes quiet when you come in, and Brunger asks no questions and pulls his oar.
endings.reward: Nothing is owed and nothing is held against the house in the west; Gunnhild cool; Brunger's heart falls.

stories.reward: Saxon friends on the Danes' side of the wall, and an ale-house where the house is known by name.

stories.title: The sign of the cross
stories.summary: From 826 Anskar works among the Danes: boys bought free and taught letters, a church by the harbour about 850, a door nailed shut in 854 and opened again, and at last a bell the heathen hold unlawful. His school needs psalters, and of the forty books he took toward Birka in 829 he has none: someone in the north has them, and a merchant who knows what a book is worth can find them among the combs.
stories.picture: A small plank church beside a harbour full of ships, an empty oak frame by its door, a priest beating a plank with a mallet, and in the foreground Danes mending nets with their backs to him.

beats.text: A thin monk is in the dealer's pen, choosing boys: Danes and Wends, twelve of them, bought for letters and not for work. The dealer thinks him a poor judge of stock and charges him accordingly.

Among the combs and whetstones a booth has a psalter, its boards gone, sold as good calfskin for scraping. Anskar set out for the Svear with nearly forty books and arrived on foot with none. This is one of them.

The church stands. Merchants baptised at Dorstadt and Hamburg go in openly; others have a priest sign them with the cross, so that they may stand inside, and leave the water for their deathbed. Anskar asks which you are.

King Horik is dead. Count Hovi has nailed the door shut and says the gods are angry at a strange god. The priest has gone south with the cup under his cloak, and the baptised merchants have gone back to saying nothing.
The young king has put the count out. The door is open, the nails are still in the post, and there is leave for a bell and no bell: only a frame of new oak, and a priest beating a plank.
At Dorstadt a woman of Birka, Catla, is giving her dead mother's silver to the poor, as the bishop taught her mother to wish. She asks whether the church at the Danes' harbour still has its roof.
The young king has given ground at Ripa for a second church. One of the boys bought out of the pen thirty years ago stands by the door, a priest now, with a sea chest and a clapper board.
Before there is a church, a fast day is kept on the ale-house bench: a Frisian crew sitting in a row before a roast pig, and the ferryman's eels the only fish in the house.

endings.how: Brought the psalter back to Anskar and paid for the bell, or carried it.
endings.text: The bell is hung in the oak frame and rung for the first time on a still morning. It carries past the second jetty and out over the inner water. The Danes mending nets look round, once. In fog, every ship in the last reach of the Slie steers by it.
endings.reward: The work 'A bell for the church' (flag unlock_work_sliesthorp_bell); flag bk_carried; Christian merchants here and at Hamburg trust the house; the last reach of the Slie one word safer in fog; men of the old faith here one step cooler.

endings.how: Took the sign of the cross to trade with both sides, sold Anskar his psalter at a fair price, and gave nothing to the bell.
endings.text: You may stand in the church and sit in the ale-house, and nobody on either bench is sure of you, which in this town is the usual thing. Anskar thanks you for the book and says he will pray for the rest of you.
endings.reward: Flag bk_knows_worth; dealings with Christian and heathen merchants here both at no loss of standing; a fair price for the psalter (about 240 d (?)).

endings.how: Kept in with Hovi's party while the door was shut: sold the psalter for scraping and drank with the men who nailed the door.
endings.text: The count is put out within the year, and his friends remember who sat with them when it was not safe. The priest remembers too. The skins take a tally well.
endings.reward: The old-faith households of the port friendly, and their sons willing crew; flag bk_lost; the church here closed to the house until a gift is made.

stories.reward: A bell on the Slie, a foot in both faiths, or the thanks of the men who lost.

stories.title: Double, on the scale
stories.summary: A Frankish blade is worth double its river price on the strand at Sliesthorp, weighed out in silver by a Dane who buys for a lord with many ships; the dealer Asulf pays in people, who are worth more further on. Every law the Frankish kings make against the trade, from the ban of 779 to the death penalty of 864, raises the price it was meant to end.
stories.picture: A folding scale held up between two men on a plank street: in one pan cut silver and an arm ring, on the board below a bare sword blade with letters inlaid along it; a stout man with a hazel switch looking on.

beats.text: A blade may be sold to a count's man and to no stranger. A smith who asks no questions wants silver by weight, and does not want to know which sea it is going to.
The toll man's rods probe the salt and the wine. What is found is forfeit. (Hidden and not found sets sw_ran_blades.)
A young Dane with an empty sword belt says what a blade would weigh in silver if you had one: double. Asulf, beside him, says what it would weigh in people. (Sets sw_buyer_known.)
Asulf makes his offer plainly: blades every summer, paid in his lots, and word of the net that is being drawn in the west.
In the war years the same buyers stand on the bank at Ripa, and pay the same.
A hilt smith in the Vik pays more than either for blades bare of hilts, and shares what they fetch.

endings.how: Sold blades to the Dane for weighed silver, and came back with more.
endings.text: The Dane's lord has his edges, and your purse has no king's face in it anywhere. In the west a clerk writes down a description of a small Frisian boat.
endings.reward: Double the river price for every blade (flag sw_buyer_known); the unlock sliesthorp.blade_buyer; the risk of flag sw_marked at every Frankish toll.

endings.how: Took Asulf's payment in captives.
endings.text: You carry people past your own king's toll in place of silver, and sell them where they are worth more. Ravn eats apart for the rest of the voyage. Asulf sends word north that the Frisian keeps a bargain.
endings.reward: Captives worth more than the silver further on; Asulf friendly; Ravn's feeling falls; the deed bought_captives wherever it is known.

endings.how: Said you carried cloth, on every call.
endings.text: Both men nod and remember your face. Nothing is asked of you again, and nothing is offered. At the tolls of the west the rods go into your salt and find salt.
endings.reward: The buyers' names all the same (flag sw_buyer_known); a clean name at the Frankish tolls.

stories.reward: A buyer for blades by name, in silver or in people, or a hold the king's men can search as often as they like.

stories.title: Not my fleets
stories.summary: From 834 a fleet goes up the Rhine to Dorestad year after year, and in the autumns after it men in this harbour sell blue cloth with Dorestad's lead seal still on it, and Dorestad people.
