King Horik sends word to the emperor that the fleets are not his and that he has taken their chiefs and killed them; a Frisian at the brook mouth can see for himself what came home.
stories.picture: A booth by a brook with blue cloth on the board, a small lead seal hanging from the selvage; behind it a fenced pen and a young woman's face at the hurdle; far off a grey king on a bench with a Frankish glass cup before him.

beats.text: This year heathen men came up the river to Dorestad and wasted it, and carried people off in their ships. The same the year after, and the year after that.
A neighbour's cloth is on the board with the seal still on it. The house that follows the raid of 834 north comes to this harbour to look for what was taken.
Behind the booth a weaver's daughter from the row behind the bank road says your boat's name. A hundred and twenty by weight; the cloth is cheaper.
The king says the fleets were not his, that he took their chiefs and killed them, and that the emperor might thank him with Frisia. He gives you a Frankish cup to drink from while he says it.
At the upper church the names you carried are read out. For some of them it is the first word in a year.

endings.how: Bought a Dorestad captive out of the pen and carried her home.
endings.text: She goes up the dam without looking back, and a house in the row behind the bank road has its loom going again by evening. The dealer remembers that Frisians pay full weight for their own.
endings.reward: The deed gave_alms (a captive redeemed); flag dn_dorestad_girl; standing at Dorestad; her kin are the house's friends for a generation.

endings.how: Bought the sealed cloth cheap and sold it.
endings.text: It is good cloth. Somebody at home knows the seal and asks where you had it, and you find you would rather not say.
endings.reward: Three bolts at half their price; flag dn_bought_dorestad_loot; the crew's heart falls; told against the house on the dams if it is known.

endings.how: Bought nothing, and carried the names home.
endings.text: You bring no one back. But who is alive at the Danes' harbour, and at what price, is said at the upper church, and families begin to count their silver.
endings.reward: Flag dn_dorestad_names; the priest at Dorestad a friend; no silver spent.

stories.reward: A neighbour bought back, cheap cloth with a seal on it, or a list of names: what a Frisian does in the harbour of the king whose fleets are not his.

stories.title: More than they can spend
stories.summary: From 991 the English king pays the fleets to go away, ten thousand pounds the first time and more each time after, and every autumn men come home to the Slie with English pennies by the sack. For a few weeks after a tribute year this is the best market for wine, glass and fine cloth on any coast. Then, about 1050, the town that grew fat on it is burned from end to end by a king of Norway, and in 1066 the Wends finish it.
stories.picture: A plank street in autumn: a young Dane in a bright new cloak pours pennies from hand to hand before a merchant's casks of wine; a moneyer at his block beside them; a high turf rampart behind the houses.

beats.text: The king's reeves gather the tribute town by town, and every house is asked for its share. (Paying sets en_paid_share.)
A man home from the fleet pours pennies from hand to hand and wants what a man with silver should have: wine, a cup that is glass. (Selling to him sets en_followed_silver.)
The moneyer weighs the English pennies and then counts them, and both come out the same. Stamped coin passes by count here now, and an old hall's cups are bought for the pot.
At Ripa the bishop has King Cnut's word read at the church door: one peace on both shores of the sea.
A charred keel as long as six boats lies under the water off the old jetties. People build again, smaller, inside the black ring.

endings.how: Came each autumn after a tribute year with wine, glass and fine cloth.
endings.text: The house's name is known among the men who were paid, and among the king's own once the Dane is king of both shores.
endings.reward: Flag en_followed_silver; the best prices of the year for luxuries, in pennies by count; the unlock sliesthorp.english_silver; helps toward flag en_cnut_peace.

endings.how: Paid the house's share of a tribute in England, and would not sell to the men it went to.
endings.text: It is an honest loss. English reeves remember a foreign house that paid like a neighbour.
endings.reward: Flag en_paid_share; standing in the English ports; no profit at the Slie.

endings.how: Came after the burning of about 1050.
endings.text: The men with pennies are over the water on the north shore now, and the old harbour is a black ring with sheep in it.
endings.reward: Nothing here. The trade goes on across the Slie.

stories.reward: The best autumn market of the age and a name among the men who were paid, or an honest loss and a name among the men who paid.

works.name: Your days on the king's wall
works.what: In 808 every leader has his length of the border wall to build, and every guest of the king owes days on it or the price of a man's days. You send your crew with spades for a week, or pay.
works.needs: To lie at Sliesthorp while the wall is building, in 808 to 810.
works.gives: The king's man at the gate knows your notch: carts for the Treene road are not kept waiting and the gate gift is the smallest that is taken. In the west it can be said of you that you built the Danes' wall.
works.picture: A line of men digging along a fresh earth bank, your four among them in Frisian cloaks, and a king's man walking the line with a tally stick.
works.source: Annales regni Francorum 808: the wall and its one gate, the work shared out among the leaders of his troops. That merchants owed days is invented (chain_reric_808 s08) (?)

works.name: A fenced plot by the brook
works.what: A plot four rods by eight, its short end to the water, given by the king's man to a merchant who will build on it before the frost and hold it over a winter. A house, a fence of wattle, and a door that locks.
works.needs: From 808; to be known at the port; the gate-man's leave.
works.gives: A stock of your own here: goods left are not aboard, bought in the cheap season and sold in the dear. A free winter berth and a roof for the crew. A factor needs it (story/unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_sliesthorp).
works.picture: A narrow fenced yard running down to the water, a new thatched house at its head, hazel rods still standing at the four corners.
works.source: Fenced plots along the brook and houses often rebuilt on wet ground (de.wikipedia Haithabu; da.wikipedia Hedeby); the plots of 808 are from chain_reric_808 and unlock_plot_sliesthorp. The measure is invented (?)

works.name: A jetty of your own
works.what: Oak piles driven into the mud off your plot and a deck of split planks out to where a loaded ship floats. Others may lie at it for a gift.
works.needs: A plot by the brook; oak from the north shore; Thormund or his heirs willing.
works.gives: No porters' fee and no waiting for a berth; a ship too deep for the strand can load here; other skippers' gifts for lying at it come to the house each summer.
works.picture: A plank jetty running out from a fenced plot into still brown water, one ship made fast at its head and a man rolling a cask along it.
works.source: Jetties up to 60 m long and plank streets running down to them (da.wikipedia Hedeby; en.wikipedia Hedeby). When the first were built was not opened (dossier 1) (?)

works.name: A bell for the church
works.what: A cast bronze bell for the empty oak frame by the church door. The young King Horik has given leave for it, though the heathen hold a bell unlawful. Copper and tin brought to the founder come off the price.
works.needs: From about 854: the church open again and the king's leave standing.
works.gives: Christian merchants trust the port and you; men of the old faith here think less of it. Heard on the water in fog, it makes the last reach of the Slie one word safer for every ship (flag unlock_work_sliesthorp_bell).
works.picture: A small bronze bell hanging in a frame of two oak posts and a beam, a priest with the rope in his hand, mist on the water behind.
works.source: Rimbert, Life of Anskar 32 (tr. Robinson 1921): the bell allowed, 'the use of which the pagans regarded as unlawful'. A whole bronze bell of about 950 was found in the harbour in 1978 (de.wikipedia Glocke von Haithabu). story/works_793.json bell; story/unlocks_793.json unlock_work_sliesthorp_bell

works.name: A stone for a partner
works.what: A tall stone set by the road at the ford, cut with runes and painted: who raised it, for whom, what he was to you, and one thing about him. Partners raise them for partners here.
works.needs: A dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership; a rune-carver; leave of whoever holds the ford.
works.gives: The crew's heart rises; Norse people of this shore know the house keeps faith with its dead, and a partner's kin stay the house's friends. An heir can read it (story/unlocks_793.json memorial_rune_stone).
works.picture: A grey standing stone by a ford, a band of red-painted runes winding up it, and one man with his hand flat on it.
works.source: 'Thorolf, Svein's retainer, raised this stone for his partner Erik... he was a steersman, a well-born warrior' (the Haithabu rune stones, about 1000; de.wikipedia Runensteine von Haithabu). The Sigtrygg stones are of about 940 (?)

ships.note: The strand is full of four- and six-oared boats: fishing, ferrying, lightering to ships that lie off. One is always for sale, and Thormund will say what is wrong with her.
ships.picture: A small tarred clinker boat on rollers above the reeds, oars laid across her thwarts, a wright tapping her planks with the back of an axe.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The house's own kind of boat is a Danish build. Ordered before leaf-fall she swims at first open water; this is the cheapest place east of Ripa to replace a lost hull.
ships.picture: A new 7-metre boat on blocks under the alders, pale split oak not yet tarred, her mast lying beside her.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: A Northman's ship of twelve oars or more, for the long northern and eastern runs: the oak, the iron and the wrights are all here. In Frankish and English waters before 878 a ship of this build is taken for a raider.
ships.picture: A long low hull half planked on the slip, her stem curling up above the wright's head, a boy heating rivets at a small fire.

ships.note: After 808 the Wends set down here sell and build their own boats, pegged with wood where the Danes rivet with iron: beamy, cheap, good in the shallow eastern lagoons.
ships.picture: A broad shallow boat on the strand with rows of wooden pegs along her planks, a Wend in a fur-edged cap sitting on her gunwale.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json baltic_coastal_boat (Slav boats pegged with treenails); Reric's merchants moved here in 808 (Annales regni Francorum)

ships.note: A hollowed log for the brook, the reeds and the inner water: an errand boat, good for eels and for nothing else.
ships.picture: A dugout nosed into the reeds, a fish trap and a pole in her.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: A king's ship was built here about 985, thirty-one metres long and under three wide. A merchant may have one built if he has leave and thirty men to feed, and should think twice: every Christian port takes her for a raider.
ships.picture: A very long, very narrow hull on the slip, sixty oar ports in a row, and the whole town small behind her.
ships.source: Hedeby 1, built about 985, 30.9 m by 2.7 m (en.wikipedia Hedeby 1; de.wikipedia Haithabu 1); ship_classes_793.json norse_longship; story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_norse_longship

sayings.text: The king has his toll at both ends of the road across the neck. A man now pays to leave one sea and pays again to reach the other.
sayings.source: story/sayings_793.json say.inv.c.sliesthorp (invented in the period's manner; from 808)

sayings.text: Give praise to the day at evening, to a woman on her pyre, / To a weapon which is tried, to a maid at wedlock, / To ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk.
sayings.source: Hávamál 81 (tr. Bellows 1923), as in lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj020. Said at the ferry when the Slie is half frozen

sayings.text: No great thing needs a man to give, / Oft little will purchase praise; / With half a loaf and a half-filled cup / A friend full fast I made.
sayings.source: Hávamál 52 (tr. Bellows 1923), as in lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj013. Gunnhild's rule for strangers

sayings.text: Tell one thy thoughts, but beware of two, / All know what is known to three.
sayings.source: Hávamál 63, lines 3-4 (tr. Bellows 1923), as in lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj015. The market's rule about prices

sayings.text: Too early to many a meeting I came, / And some too late have I sought; / The beer was all drunk, or not yet brewed; / Little the loathed man finds.
sayings.source: Hávamál 66 (tr. Bellows 1923), as in lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj016

sayings.text: Here silver has no face. It has a weight, and the weight has a cut in it where somebody did not trust it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; silver by weight and the knife nick before the pennies of about 825 (economy/silver_coin.md)

sayings.text: A Frisian counts his pennies, a Svea weighs them, a Dane bites them, and the Wend asks what else you have.
A stranger said of us that we sing like dogs, only worse. He had not heard the dogs.
sayings.source: invented, turning Ibrahim ibn Yaqub's remark of the 960s (en.wikipedia Hedeby): 'never did I hear singing fouler than that of these people: a rumbling from their throats, like a dog's but more bestial'. From about 965

sayings.text: Moneyer's joke: the letters say Dorestad. I have never been there. Neither, by now, has anyone.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Hedeby pennies copy Dorestad's long after 863 (realms/denmark.md; da.wikipedia Hedebymønter). From 864

sayings.text: He took the cross to trade with the Christians and the hammer to trade with the rest, and God and Thor are both waiting to see which he dies in.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Rimbert, Life of Anskar 24: many took the sign of the cross and put off baptism until their deathbed. From about 850

sayings.text: A wall with one gate is a purse with one mouth.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Annales regni Francorum 808

easter_eggs.text: At low water a line of squared logs shows across the narrows of the Slie: boxes of oak filled with stone, older than anyone living. The ferryman knows the gap. Nobody remembers which king built it.
easter_eggs.source: The timber sea barrier off Reesholm, built about 737 to 740; how ships passed it is not known (de.wikipedia Schlei-Seesperrwerk)

easter_eggs.text: A short pull north of the log fence a hill has long houses on it and ships drawn up below: the king's watch on the mouth of the Slie.
easter_eggs.source: Füsing, a garrison and fleet station of about 700 to 1000, 2 km north of the barrier (de.wikipedia Wikingersiedlung von Füsing)

easter_eggs.text: In the summer of 810 a carter in from the west has a story nobody believes: the emperor has a beast as big as a house with a snake for a nose, a gift from a king beyond Rome, and it has just died.
easter_eggs.source: Annales regni Francorum 810: the elephant sent by the caliph died while Charles waited on Godfred

easter_eggs.text: About 890 a Northman on the jetty says that these lands, Jutland and the islands, are where the English lived before they came to Britain. An Englishman beside him looks round at the reeds as if he had lost something here.
easter_eggs.source: Ohthere in Alfred's Orosius: 'in these lands the English lived before they came hither' (Hakluyt 1893; texts_793.json ohthere)

easter_eggs.text: The comb-makers' street is white underfoot. A child could fill a ship with the offcuts of antler, and in eleven hundred years someone will count them.
easter_eggs.source: Over 340,000 pieces of comb-makers' waste were dug at Hedeby (en.wikipedia Hedeby; de.wikipedia Haithabu)

easter_eggs.text: From about 940 a tall stone by the ford says in Swedish-looking runes that Asfrid made this monument for Sigtrygg, her son and Gnupa's. It is cut on a rock that already bore older marks nobody can read.
easter_eggs.source: The large Sigtrygg stone, in Swedish runes on a rock with older marks, found broken at the ford between the two Noors (de.wikipedia Runensteine von Haithabu)

easter_eggs.text: South of the houses, from about 900, a mound has a boat's stem showing through the turf. Three men lie in a chamber under her keel with their swords and a glass beaker, and three horses in a pit beside them. Nobody says whose men they were.
easter_eggs.source: The boat chamber grave, found 1908, of about 900; no other like it is known (de.wikipedia Bootkammergrab von Haithabu)

easter_eggs.text: In the 960s a dark, careful stranger from Spain walks the plank streets writing nothing down and missing nothing. He is troubled that the men paint their eyes, as the women do, and that it suits them.
easter_eggs.source: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub of Tortosa (en.wikipedia Hedeby; Ibrahim ibn Yaqub): both sexes paint their eyes; women may divorce

easter_eggs.text: About 950 a bronze bell goes into the harbour mud off the church jetty: dropped from a boat, or put there. It will lie whole for a thousand years and ring again.
easter_eggs.source: The bell of Haithabu, about 950, found in the harbour in 1978: the oldest whole ringing bell in northern Europe (de.wikipedia Glocke von Haithabu). How it came there is not known

easter_eggs.text: The goldsmith's boy coughs and his hands shake. His master gilds with gold rubbed into quicksilver and burned off over the fire, and nobody has connected the two.
easter_eggs.source: Mercury from fire-gilding in the goldsmiths' workshops (en.wikipedia Hedeby; de.wikipedia Haithabu). The boy is invented

easter_eggs.text: After 1050 a charred keel as long as six boats lies under the water off the old jetties: a king's longship, filled with dry wood and sent burning into the harbour.
easter_eggs.source: Hedeby 1, built about 985, burnt to the waterline as a fire ship; the fire is dated 990 to 1010 on one page and 1050 on another (en.wikipedia Hedeby 1; de.wikipedia Haithabu 1) (?)

easter_eggs.text: After 1066 the people over the water have a name for the empty ring of turf: the old fort. Sheep graze inside it, and the brook still runs out where the jetties were.
easter_eggs.source: Once the town was gone the people called the ring Oldenburg (de.wikipedia Haithabu)

unlocks.gives: She answers for you: no one on the strand may treat the house as hostless. Free lodging for the crew, and the ale-house's rumours fresh on every call. Her daughter keeps the stick after her, at half the warmth.
